offence_severity: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 5,000/- for the offence committed under Section 376(2)(g) IPC, 1-year rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/- for the offence committed under Section 506(1) IPC and 1-year imprisonment for the offence committed under Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Woman Act
physical_harm: Injuries on her person, loss of virginity, and abrasions on the private parts of the victim
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 376(2)(g) and 506(1) of IPC and Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Woman Act; finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The prosecutrix's statement under Section 164 CrPC, the FIR lodged on the same day, the medical expert's testimony about the victim's injuries, and the corroboration from the victim's mother and aunt.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that despite the prosecutrix and her mother and aunt turning hostile during cross-examination, their evidence was still reliable and corroborated by other evidence such as the FIR, the medical report, and the statement under Section 164 CrPC.

legal_representation.accused: Rahul Shyam Bhandari, Ms. G. Priytadarshini, Satyam Pathak, Dr. Ratneshwar Chakma
legal_representation.state: V. Krishnamurthy, Sr. A.A.G., D. Kumanan, Mrs. Deepa. S, Sheikh F. Kalia, Veshal Tyagi, Ms. Richa Vishwakarma

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed

appeal_history.high_court: Dismissed the appeal and upheld the findings of the trial court

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the victim and her mother and aunt fully supported the prosecution case, the FIR was lodged immediately, the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC was recorded, and the medical expert confirmed injuries. The prosecution emphasized the corroboration of the victim's version with the FIR, the statement under Section 164 CrPC, and the medical evidence.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the victim and her mother and aunt turned hostile during cross-examination and did not support the prosecution case. They also claimed that the medical evidence did not support the prosecution's case and relied on the judgment in Rai Sandeep alias Deepu v. State (NCT of Delhi) to challenge the conviction.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the evidence of a hostile witness cannot be rejected in toto merely because the prosecution treated them as hostile, and that relevant parts of their testimony can be used if found dependable upon careful scrutiny.
precedent_relied_upon: Khujji @ Surendra Tiwari v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1991) 3 SCC 627; Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana (1976) 1 SCC 389; Sri Rabindra Kumar Dey v. State of Orissa (1976) 4 SCC 233; Syad Akbar v. State of Karnataka (1980) 1 SCC 30; C. Muniappan and Others v. State of Tamil Nadu (2010) 9 SCC 567; Vinod Kumar v. State of Punjab (2015) 3 SCC 220; Rajesh Yadav and Another v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2022) 12 SCC 200
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the trial court's findings were upheld by the High Court and the Supreme Court.
